answerBody: Assume governments adopt binding conditional approval for frontier AI development and deployment, including independent evaluation and possible time-limited delays. The unresolved design choice is the trigger for that regime: should obligations attach primarily before training or deployment based on measurable inputs and projected scale, such as compute, model size, autonomy goals, or developer capacity, or should they attach only after evaluators observe specified hazardous capabilities in a model or system? Choose the governing trigger default for frontier oversight and defend it under uncertainty.
rationale: Contextual delta: the selected Spring chose binding conditional approval, but its mixed phrase “thresholds or showing hazardous capabilities” leaves the trigger unresolved. This follow-up does not replay Genesis’s binding-vs-competition default; it assumes binding oversight and asks what activates it. There is no prior Autumn. Incompatible answers remain defensible: ex ante scale/input triggers are administrable and early, while observed-capability triggers are more risk-proximate and may avoid overbreadth. A compromise cannot evade the fork because regulators still need a default when capability evidence is absent or incomplete. Durable basis: EU AI Act duties attach to systemic-risk GPAI classification and require evaluation/reporting; UK AISI has used inputs such as training compute and expected accessibility; Frontier Model Forum notes compute thresholds can over- and under-include, while capability/risk thresholds connect more directly to hazards.  Word-counting capability confirmed answerBody is within range.
